newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Poll shows Russians don't trust Yeltsin,back Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows Russians don't trust Yeltsin,back Lebed.

text.p: Ousted security adviser Alexander Lebed is Russia's most trusted politician and fewer than one in four people trust President Boris Yeltsin, according to an opinion poll published on Thursday.

The survey, carried out by the Russian Independent Institute for Social and National Issues in the last week of December, showed that more than half the 2200 respondents across Russia did not trust the president.
The survey, published by the Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper, showed only 22.6 percent trusted Yeltsin, who was re-elected last summer but is now recovering in hospital from pneumonia.
Lebed, a former paratroop commander sacked by Yeltsin as his national security adviser in October for openly seeking to become president, was far ahead of his nearest rival on 58.4 percent.

Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov has the trust of 42.7 percent of respondents and liberal economist Grigory Yavlinsky was trusted by 34.9 percent, the survey showed. A young liberal regional leader, Boris Nemtsov, was next with 34.4 percent.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, who was defeated by Yeltsin in the election runoff last July, was in fifth place with the trust of 29.9 percent of respondents.
Lebed has been calling for Yeltsin to step down since the president fell ill last week and says he has no doubts he would win an early election.
Yeltsin was taken to hospital with pneumonia on January 8, only two weeks after his return to work in the Kremlin following a quintuple bypass operation on November 5.
Asked how they thought various politicians would do if new presidential elections were held immediately, Lebed got 25.9 percent and Zyuganov 20.3 percent.
Yeltsin is barred under the constitution from seeking a third presidential term but he was seen getting 14.6 percent.

Respondents were also asked to predict the outcome of an election on schedule in the year 2000. Lebed again had the lead, with 26.1 percent, followed by Zyuganov with 20.2 percent and Yavlinsky with 11.6 percent.

Russia's Prime Minsiter Viktor Chernomyrdin, who is seen by some politicians as a potential successor to Yeltsin, won the trust of 23.9 percent of the respondents, but his chances of becoming a president in 2000 were lower at only 7.1 percent.
Flamboyant ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky was not on the list of the eight most trusted politicians and only 4.4 percent of respondents said he could become a president in 2000.

A peace deal with Chechen separatists, signed by Lebed last year ending to the conflict in which tens of thousands were killed, was named the most postitive event of 1996 by 80 percent of respondents in the same survey.
